fragments.text: Hello, my name is David Leslie. I'm a professor of ethics technology and society at Queen Mary University of London and director of ethics and responsible innovation research at the Alan Turing Institute. I'm so grateful today to be talking to you for AI for IA about advancing data justice research and practice a project that has been undertaken by my research team at the Alan Turing Institute for the last few years. And what I'll do today is I'll offer a bit of an intro into this project, which over the past couple of years has been first supported by the Global Partnership on AI. Also a base from the UK government has supported the expansion of the project and EPSRC, the UK's engineering and physical sciences research council has also supported the work.

fragments.fragment_id: 0153_e1PJUdUiMXk_David Leslie - Advancing Data Justice Research and Practice_0002
fragments.source_video: 0153_e1PJUdUiMXk_David Leslie - Advancing Data Justice Research and Practice
fragments.text: So just to give you a basic overview of the project itself in 2021, June, my team applied for a grant through GP to study social justice implications of globally ramifying data vacation. The project advancing data justice research and practice aimed to widen the lens of current thinking around data justice and to provide actionable resources to help policymakers practitioners and impacted communities gain a broader understanding of what equitable freedom promoting and rights sustaining data collection governance and use should look like in an increasingly dynamic and global data innovation ecosystem. So when we engage the project initially, we had committed to carrying out an integrated literature view and annotated bibliography, a repository of use cases that demonstrated the ways in which civil society organizations were actually carrying out activities and practices of data justice.

fragments.text: And also three practical guidances on data justice for policymakers for developers and impacted communities. And the project had initially started quite small actually, it was just a team, a research team of maybe four or five people. We were able to then apply for secondary grants that enabled us to take on policy pilot partners from around the globe who became our research, our co researchers and co designers of the research and you can see in front of you, these are just some of our collaborators, the main policy pilot partners that we had. You can see that they stretched from up to a row of Zealand through to India, Pakistan, Uganda, Cameroon, Brazil, Chile and Bolivia. And basically what we did with the partners is as we were developing the research, our partners are basically civil society organizations who did kind of grassroots engagements with their communities.
